note: fBOMB burns 1% of the transferred amount on a taxed transfer. A single taxed transfer emits TWO Transfer events with the SAME sender: floor(amount * 99 / 100) to the intended recipient and the remaining amount - floor(amount * 99 / 100) == ceil(amount / 100) to the zero address. Both legs are visible in the receipt, so the split can be replayed from eth_getLogs alone without tracing. Verified across 49 burn-leg transfers in blocks 501992804..502292803: the identity transferToRecipient == floor(amount*99/100) held on EVERY sample with no exceptions. Because the fee is a floored integer division rather than an exact percentage, the realised rate is 100 bps only up to a rounding residue of at most one base unit -- for the cited transaction the exact ratio is 132650913076533859510000/1326509130765338595071 bps, which exceeds 100 by ~2.19e-18 bps. feeBps carries the nominal 100. NOT every transfer is taxed: the exemption is on the RECIPIENT side, and some addresses receive fBOMB with a single untaxed Transfer event. That does not weaken the routing classification, because transfers in and out of the vrAMM-fBOMB/WETH pool cited above ARE taxed -- the cited transaction is the pool itself paying out, and the counterparty receives only 99%. IMPORTANT: this is a SEPARATE deployment from the fBOMB already listed on chain 8453. The address is the same but the contracts are independent (totalSupply here is 4429485470445692295835488, different from every other chain), so the tax had to be evidenced on this chain in its own right and a listing on one chain says nothing about another. Failure modes by position in a router path: (1) fBOMB as INPUT or INTERMEDIATE -- the destination pool receives only 99% of amountSent, so pool.swap(amount0Out, ...) reverts K() because the demanded output assumed the full amountSent; (2) fBOMB as TERMINAL OUTPUT -- no next pool and no K() revert, but the user receives 99% of the quoted amountOut, silently violating the minAmountOut slippage promise (delivered < quoted). Both modes are unsafe.
